items.prose: Burning unseasoned green pine branches rich in turpentine resin deposited a heavy black varnish of wood creosote across two hundred sides of pork bacon. The bitter tar imparted a caustic turpentine taste that caused severe stomach cramps when consumed.

Excessive firebox draft allowed flame tongues to lick directly into the smoking chamber (95°C). The meat fat dripped into glowing coals, creating thick clouds of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons that left jerky strips smelling like asphalt roof shingles.

A maze-track smoke generator loaded with dry hickory sawdust maintained a flawless 28°C cold smoke for seventy-two hours. Phenolic vapor fractions penetrated deep into forty cured hams, giving a mahogany gloss and outstanding anti-microbial protection.

A kitchen orderly confused grams and ounces, adding four times the safe dosage of sodium nitrite (Prague Powder #1) to a batch of blood sausages. Three squad members who ate the sausages developed blue lips and dizziness from acute methemoglobinemia.

Rapid drying in a drafty, overheated smokehouse baked an impenetrable, leather-hard crust onto the outside of thirty-pound venison hams. Moisture trapped around the femur bone could not escape; anaerobic putrefaction rotted the ham interior into liquefied stench.

A hole in the cheesecloth intake screen allowed green blowflies (*Lucilia sericata*) into the cold-smoke chamber during a draft lull. Flies struck twelve sides of hanging bacon, depositing thousands of egg clusters in meat crevices before smoke was rekindled.

Bacon bellies soaked in crude sorghum molasses cure were hung too close to the floor heat baffle. Heat caramelized and charred the surface sugars into a blackened, bitter crust that flaked off in frying pans and filled the dining hall with pungent sweet smoke.
